title: The 1.5°C Goal Slips Away, but the Door Is Not Closed
title_zh: 1.5°C 目标渐行渐远，但大门并未关闭
source_name: UN News — “Global warming will breach 1.5°C – but deep, fast cuts can still bring it back” (21 Oct 2026)
summary_zh: 联合国环境规划署（UNEP）10 月 21 日发布《2026 年排放差距报告》，指出全球升温已无法避免突破《巴黎协定》设定的 1.5°C 上限。按现行政策，本世纪升温可能达到 2.8°C；即使各国完全兑现气候承诺，也将升温约 2.6°C。报告提出“最低程度超标”情景：本世纪中叶升温峰值控制在 1.7–1.8°C，到 2100 年回落至 1.5°C，但这需要全球排放到 2030 年减少 18%、2035 年减少 45%（相对 2025 年），并大规模清除二氧化碳。报告也看到希望：可再生能源快速发展，许多国家的气候政策已带来实际减排。下月在土耳其安塔利亚举行的 COP31 气候大会将是关键节点。
paragraphs: For more than a decade, the number 1.5 has been at the heart of global climate policy. In the 2015 Paris Agreement, nearly every country promised to try to keep the rise in global temperature below 1.5°C compared with pre-industrial times. This week, however, a new United Nations report delivered a sobering message: that goal can no longer be met without at least a temporary “overshoot”.

The Emissions Gap Report 2026, published on 21 October by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), measures the difference between what countries have promised and what science says is necessary. Its conclusion is that the gap remains enormous. If governments simply continue with their current policies, the planet could warm by as much as 2.8°C this century. Even if every national climate plan is fully carried out, warming would still reach about 2.6°C. The authors note that these projections are worse than last year’s, partly because the United States has withdrawn from the Paris deal.

Yet the report is not entirely pessimistic. It describes a “lowest possible” overshoot scenario in which temperatures peak at around 1.7 to 1.8°C by the middle of the century and then gradually fall back to 1.5°C by 2100. Achieving this would require global emissions to drop by 18 per cent by 2030 and by 45 per cent by 2035, compared with 2025 levels — far deeper cuts than current national pledges would deliver. It would also depend on removing large amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere over the coming decades.

There are genuine reasons for hope. Since 2015, renewable energy has expanded rapidly, and the use of coal and oil has grown more slowly than experts once predicted. In many countries, climate policies have already produced measurable reductions in emissions. “Overshoot is not surrender,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said, arguing that the excess warming can still be kept small and short.

The timing matters. Next month, governments will gather in Antalya, Türkiye, for the COP31 climate summit, where they will begin a new review of their collective progress. Whether they respond with stronger commitments may determine how far, and for how long, the world exceeds a limit it once hoped never to cross.
